questions.question: What is the difference between absolute units and relative units?
options: Absolute units are always larger than relative units
Absolute units are fixed sizes (like pixels), while relative units scale based on parent elements or viewport size
Relative units are fixed sizes, while absolute units scale
There is no difference
questions.explanation: Absolute units (like pixels and points) are fixed sizes that don't change. Relative units (like em, rem, %, vw, vh) scale based on their parent element or the viewport size.

questions.question: Which of the following is an absolute unit?
options: em
rem
px (pixels)
% (percentage)
questions.explanation: Pixels (px) are an absolute unit - they represent a fixed size. em, rem, and % are all relative units.

questions.question: What does 'em' stand for and what is it relative to?
options: Element margin - relative to the element's margin
Element measure - relative to the element's width
Relative to the font-size of the parent element
Relative to the root element's font-size
questions.explanation: 'em' is relative to the font-size of the parent element. For example, 2em means 2 times the size of the parent's font.

questions.question: What does 'rem' stand for and what is it relative to?
options: Root element margin - relative to the root's margin
Relative to the font-size of the root element (usually the <html> element)
Relative to the parent element's font-size
Relative to the viewport width
questions.explanation: 'rem' stands for 'root em' and is relative to the font-size of the root element (usually the <html> element). This makes it more predictable than 'em'.

questions.question: What does 'vw' stand for?
options: Viewport width - relative to 1% of the width of the browser window
Viewport height - relative to 1% of the height of the browser window
Variable width - a fixed width unit
Vertical width - relative to the parent element
questions.explanation: 'vw' stands for viewport width. It's relative to 1% of the width of the browser window. For example, 30vw means 30% of the viewport width.

questions.question: What does 'vh' stand for?
options: Viewport height - relative to 1% of the height of the browser window
Viewport width - relative to 1% of the width of the browser window
Variable height - a fixed height unit
Vertical height - relative to the parent element
questions.explanation: 'vh' stands for viewport height. It's relative to 1% of the height of the browser window. For example, 50vh means 50% of the viewport height.

questions.question: What is the percentage (%) unit relative to?
options: The viewport size
The root element
The parent element
A fixed pixel value
questions.explanation: The percentage (%) unit is relative to the parent element. For example, width: 100% means 100% of the parent element's width.

questions.question: What does 'fr' stand for in CSS Grid?
options: Fraction - a fixed unit
Fractional units of the available space within the parent element
Frame - relative to the viewport
Font ratio - relative to font size
questions.explanation: 'fr' stands for 'fraction' and represents fractional units of the available space within the parent element. It's used in CSS Grid for flexible column/row sizing.

options: The container will be 50 pixels wide
The container will be 50% of the viewport width
The container will be 50% of the parent element's width
The container will be 50% of the viewport height
questions.explanation: 50vw means 50% of the viewport width. The 'vw' unit is always relative to the viewport width, regardless of what property it's used for.

questions.question: According to the CSS Units resource, what is the recommended approach for responsive design?
options: Always use absolute units like pixels
Use relative units when possible so pages can scale and be resized on-the-fly
Mix absolute and relative units equally
Never use relative units
questions.explanation: The resource recommends using relative units when possible for responsive designs. This allows pages to scale and be resized on-the-fly, making them work better on different screen sizes.

options: 1.5px
16px
It depends on the root element
questions.explanation: Since 'em' is relative to the parent's font-size, 1.5em means 1.5 times the parent's font-size. 1.5 × 16px = 24px.

questions.question: Which unit would be best for creating a full-height section that always takes up the entire viewport height?
options: 100px
100vh
100em
questions.explanation: 100vh means 100% of the viewport height, which is perfect for creating a full-height section that always takes up the entire browser window height, regardless of content.
